canonical_definition: Long-Context Understanding refers to the capacity of language models to process, reason over, and integrate information from extended input sequences—such as lengthy documents (e.g., research papers, legal contracts), multi-turn dialogues, or streaming data—without reliance on chunking, retrieval, or segmentation. This construct encompasses the ability to handle sequences exceeding typical training context lengths, maintain coherence across distributed contextual elements, and perform tasks like question answering, comprehension, or multimodal reasoning that demand sustained attention to long-range dependencies. While operationalized variably across studies (e.g., via closed-ended tasks, NIAH PLUS testing, or dialogue history retention), it consistently emphasizes holistic processing of inputs far beyond standard context windows while preserving functional utility.
